# Maritime OOD Detection — Client Update

*Image-level AUROC (Slide 4 also reports inference speed). For each experiment the configuration is chosen on the validation split; both the validation AUROC and the held-out test AUROC are reported. Higher is better; 0.5 = chance.*

---

## Slide 1 — Single-Modality vs Fused RGB + IR

*Backbone: ViT-L self-supervised on ShipSpotting RGB + synthetic IR (generated by FLUX) — the **Standard** backbone (Slides 2–3).*

**How it was performed:**
- Single modality — PCA fitted on one modality only (**RGB** or **IR**).
- Pooled — PCA fitted on **both** modalities together in one shared subspace.

| Single modality | val / test AUROC |
|---|---|
| RGB | 0.8664 / 0.8773 |
| IR (synthetic) | 0.8340 / 0.8217 |

| Pooled (RGB ∪ IR, one subspace) | val / test AUROC | Δ vs single (val / test) |
|---|---|---|
| Combined (RGB + IR) | 0.8544 / 0.8547 | — |
| ↳ RGB-only subset | 0.8673 / 0.8669 | +0.0009 / −0.0104 |
| ↳ IR-only subset | 0.8407 / 0.8425 | +0.0067 / +0.0208 |

**Takeaway:** One shared subspace serves both modalities without per-modality tuning. Pooling lifts IR (test 0.8217 → 0.8425) and slightly lowers RGB (0.8773 → 0.8669).

---

## Slide 2 — Improving Robustness on Low-Quality / Low-Resolution IR

*Two ViT-L backbones — **Standard**: self-supervised on RGB + synthetic IR; **Degradation-aware**: further trained on an 80/20 mix of degraded and non-degraded synthetic IR.*

**How it was performed (synthetic IR):**
- **degraded** = Real-ESRGAN corruption applied to IR, approximating real-world IR conditions (low quality / low resolution).
- **fit → eval** = the IR the subspace is fitted on → the IR it is scored on. Three pairings, each run on both backbones:
  - **non-degraded → non-degraded** — ideal upper bound.
  - **non-degraded → degraded** — robustness to unseen degradation.
  - **degraded → degraded** — the realistic real-world case.

| IR scenario (fit → eval) | val / test AUROC (Standard) | val / test AUROC (Degradation-aware) | Δ val / test AUROC |
|---|---|---|---|
| non-degraded → non-degraded | 0.8340 / 0.8217 | 0.8703 / 0.8814 | +0.0363 / +0.0597 |
| non-degraded → degraded | 0.7155 / 0.7104 | 0.8371 / 0.8358 | +0.1216 / +0.1254 |
| degraded → degraded | 0.5932 / 0.5878 | 0.8516 / 0.8600 | +0.2584 / +0.2722 |

**Takeaway:** Degradation-aware pretraining makes the detector robust on low-quality IR. The Standard baseline reaches only 0.5878 test, while Degradation-aware lifts it to 0.8600 (+0.2722).

---

## Slide 3 — Generalizing to a Real IR Dataset (Infiray)

*Same two ViT-L backbones (Standard / Degradation-aware), now applied to **Infiray** — a second, independent dataset of **real** IR ship images, vs ShipSpotting's synthetic IR.*

**How the eval datasets are built:**
- **Cross-domain** — PCA is fitted on **ShipSpotting** (no Infiray training), then used to score Infiray. Normal (ID) = all **7 Infiray categories**; anomalies (OOD) = the **4 held-out ShipSpotting anomaly classes** (degraded IR). **11 categories total (7 ID + 4 OOD).** The best configuration from ShipSpotting's validation split does not transfer, so it is re-selected on an Infiray validation split.
- **In-domain** — PCA is fitted on **Infiray**. Of its **7 categories**, the **5 most common = normal (ID)** and the **2 rarest = anomalies (OOD)**. **7 categories total (5 ID + 2 OOD).**

**Cross-domain (PCA fit on ShipSpotting → score Infiray, re-tuned):**

| ShipSpotting PCA fit | val / test AUROC (Standard) | val / test AUROC (Degradation-aware) | Δ val / test AUROC |
|---|---|---|---|
| non-degraded IR | 0.7130 / 0.6916 | 0.7026 / 0.6730 | −0.0104 / −0.0186 |
| degraded IR | 0.6475 / 0.6487 | 0.6914 / 0.6811 | +0.0439 / +0.0324 |

**In-domain (PCA fit on Infiray):**

| Infiray PCA fit | val / test AUROC (Standard) | val / test AUROC (Degradation-aware) | Δ val / test AUROC |
|---|---|---|---|
| real IR | 0.7736 / 0.7323 | 0.9434 / 0.9254 | +0.1698 / +0.1931 |

**Takeaways:**
- A subspace fitted on ShipSpotting must be re-tuned on Infiray to transfer. Re-tuning recovers both backbones to ~0.65–0.69 test.
- The degradation-aware backbone transfers to the real IR dataset, while the standard one generalizes only weakly. In-domain test AUROC 0.9254 vs 0.7323 (+0.1931).

---

## Slide 4 — Speed vs Accuracy across Model Sizes (ViT-S / B / L)

**How it was performed:**
- Same pipeline, generic ImageNet-pretrained **DINOv2 ViT-S / ViT-B / ViT-L**, on the hardest scenario (**degraded → degraded IR**).
- Speed on an **NVIDIA A100 (40 GB)**, 224 px, FP32, end-to-end, averaged after warm-up:
  - **Throughput** — img/s at **batch 16** (bulk rate, higher = better), over 320 images.
  - **Latency** — time for **one image** at **batch 1** (real-time, lower = better), broken into feature extraction + SubspaceAD scoring.

*Latency @ b1 is split into its two inference stages: **feature extraction** (DINOv2 forward) and **SubspaceAD** scoring (PCA reconstruction residual).*

| Model | Params | val / test AUROC | Throughput @ b16 (img/s) | Feature extraction @ b1 (ms) | SubspaceAD @ b1 (ms) | Total latency @ b1 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ViT-S | 22 M | 0.6667 / 0.6280 | 215 | 11.7 | 0.1 | 11.8 |
| ViT-B | 87 M | 0.6842 / 0.6029 | 154 | 12.6 | 1.2 | 13.8 |
| ViT-L | 304 M | 0.6806 / 0.6619 | 69 | 25.4 | 1.9 | 27.3 |

**Takeaways:**
- ViT-S offers the best speed–accuracy trade-off. As the fastest and smallest model (215 img/s, 22 M params), it even beats the 4× larger ViT-B (0.6280 vs 0.6029 test) and trails ViT-L by only 0.0339 (0.6619) while running 3.1× faster.
- **SubspaceAD scoring is near-free.** It adds only 0.1–1.9 ms (<10%) on top of feature extraction. The DINOv2 forward dominates the per-image cost end to end.
